patterns: what happens if you drop the baton
entries.answer: A relay passes a baton between runners, each running one leg, and the team result is the sum of the four times rather than the best individual time. That is why the fourth runner, the anchor, is usually the strongest, since a fast first three can absorb one poor leg. The rules are strict about where the exchange happens, inside a marked zone, and handing the baton rather than throwing it, because an invalid pass disqualifies the team.

patterns: why is the take-off board so close
entries.answer: The long jump is a horizontal jump measured from the take-off board to the nearest mark in the sand, and the technique is a run-up that has to be consistent and a take-off that has to be in front of the board rather than after it. The physics is that a longer take-off board distance gives a faster approach but reduces the margin for error, which is why the board position is the technical work. Most faults are called for touching the board or the sand, rather than for a short jump.

entries.answer: The triple jump is three linked jumps, hop, step and jump, and the discipline is that each phase has a purpose rather than being three equal bounds. The hop takes off and absorbs on the same leg, the step extends the stride, and the final jump converts the run into height and distance. It is the harder event of the two jumps, because the athlete must commit to a landing position in the air before knowing how far the previous phase carried them.

entries.answer: A sprint start is the launch from the blocks, and it is worth more time than most athletes expect, since the difference between a good and a poor start is a fifth of a second. The three-point stance is standard: rear foot about two foot-lengths back and roughly a hand's width ahead of the front. The reaction time dominates the first phase, so a false start is penalised even when the athlete was ready, and the rules allow one false start before disqualification in most competitions.
